strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies and formalizes 'multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing', which is clearly distinguished from single-agent hallucination studied in prior work, and this framing is a genuine contribution to the MAS reliability literature.

Thorough diagnostic analysis: the turn-wise, layer-wise, and token-wise attention studies (Figures 2, 5, 10, 11; Tables 1, 12) provide systematic empirical evidence linking attention degradation over agent turns to hallucination propagation, and the identification of 'unimodal attention peak' vision tokens in middle layers is an interesting and verifiable insight generalized across six VLMs.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: results span eight benchmarks, four MAS structures, ten base models (7B–34B), ablations of both components, hyperparameter sensitivity (Tables 9–11), and the impact of the number of agent turns, which is unusually broad coverage for this area.

Practical method design details: the Key-Norm alternative to attention-score-based token selection addresses the Flash-Attention incompatibility issue and is validated against Value-Norm baselines (Table 7), and a new hallucination snowballing score (HS) is proposed to quantify propagation.

Comparisons against five recent hallucination-mitigation methods (MemVR, VISTA, FarSight, DeCo, TAME) show they fail or even degrade in MAS settings, supporting the paper's claim that propagation requires a distinct solution.
weaknesses: The 'plug-and-play' claim is overstated: the visual relay tokens are contextualized by a trainable lightweight transformer block (Eq. 1) requiring a two-stage training pipeline (Table 8), so the method is not training-free; the cost of retraining/adapting this module for each base VLM and its data requirements are not clearly quantified.

The multi-agent setup is somewhat synthetic: MAS structures are constructed around single-image QA/captioning benchmarks with repeated agent turns, which may not reflect realistic multi-agent deployments (e.g., heterogeneous tasks, tool use, text-only agents); the ecological validity of the snowballing phenomenon in such settings deserves more discussion.

The causal link between attention reduction and hallucination snowballing is largely correlational; Figures 1b–1c show co-occurrence, but the analysis does not rule out confounders (e.g., longer contexts diluting attention regardless of hallucination).

The proposed HS metric (Eq. 7) depends on a judge model's centesimal hallucination scores and a somewhat arbitrary sigmoid weighting of propagation distance; its validity and correlation with human judgments are not validated, and it is used as the headline metric in Table 5.

Some method components appear heuristic (temperature scaling in middle layers, reallocation coefficients α1/α2, salience threshold ω), and while hyperparameter tables are provided, the design choices lack deeper justification; it is unclear how sensitive results are across model families.

Missing efficiency analysis: the paper does not report the computational/memory overhead of ViF (extra transformer block, additional relay tokens, modified attention computation) relative to baselines, which matters for a claimed lightweight method.

Some comparisons may disadvantage baselines: single-agent methods (MemVR, DeCo, etc.) were designed for different settings, and their degradation in MAS could partly stem from suboptimal adaptation rather than a fundamental limitation; the paper's interpretation is plausible but not fully controlled.

Writing has minor clarity issues (e.g., 'alternative of attention score based strategy', Figure numbering out of order with Figure 4 appearing before Figure 3), and the abstract/tables are dense with small-font numbers that are hard to parse.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a relatively novel problem: multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing, and distinguishes it from single-model hallucination via two interacting mechanisms (intrinsic hallucination and propagation), which is a timely and relevant framing for VLM-based MAS.

The diagnostic analyses (turn-wise, layer-wise, and token-wise attention decomposition; vision-token subset ablations across shallow/middle/deep layers) are systematic and reasonably well designed, and are validated across six VLMs in the appendix rather than a single model.

Broad empirical coverage: eight benchmarks, four MAS structures, ten base VLMs spanning 7B to 34B, with ablations on relay-token ratios, attention reallocation, and key hyperparameters, plus a Key-Norm alternative for Flash-Attention models where attention scores are unavailable.

Comparison against five existing hallucination-mitigation methods in the MAS setting, and a dedicated snowballing score (HS) that attempts to measure both severity and propagation rather than only endpoint accuracy.
weaknesses: The 'plug-and-play' claim is overstated: the method requires training an additional lightweight transformer block via a two-stage training pipeline (Table 8), which contradicts the lightweight/plug-and-play characterization and complicates adoption and reproducibility.

The proposed HS metric is self-defined and relies on a judge model; its validity, calibration, and correlation with human judgments are not validated, yet headline claims (e.g., '30-40% snowballing reduction') rest substantially on it. Gains on the original metrics are modest (2-4% average).

The mechanistic analysis establishes correlation between declining visual attention allocation and hallucination snowballing, but the causal link is not convincingly established; the hypothesis about unimodal-peak tokens as the visual information carrier is supported mainly by ablation and visualization rather than direct evidence.

No statistical significance testing or multiple-run variance is reported anywhere, despite relatively small margins on several benchmarks (e.g., CHAIR_, POPE, MM-Vet differences of fractions of a point), making it hard to assess reliability of the improvements.

Core analyses are conducted primarily on one model/benchmark pair (LLaVA-NeXT-7B on POPE) in the main text, and generality is deferred to the appendix; several baselines in Table 5 appear weaker in MAS settings than expected (some below the raw baseline), which raises questions about how fairly the comparison methods were tuned for the multi-agent setting.

Method design involves several hand-tuned components and hyperparameters (salience threshold ω, temperature τ, reallocation coefficients α1/α2, buffer tokens, subset definitions), with optimal values found empirically; sensitivity and cross-model transfer of these choices are not thoroughly discussed.

Writing and presentation could be tighter: the motivation and method sections repeat similar claims multiple times, and the overall contribution is primarily empirical/observational with limited conceptual or theoretical depth beyond the proposed heuristic.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem identification: the paper formalizes 'multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing', distinguishing it from single-model hallucination, which is a genuinely new angle in VLM-based MAS research.

The requisite analysis (Section 2) is thorough and informative: turn-wise, layer-wise, and token-wise attention analyses, plus ablations of five vision-token subsets across shallow/middle/deep layers, provide a solid empirical basis (generalized across six VLMs in the appendix) for the method design.

Comprehensive evaluation: eight benchmarks, four MAS structures, ten base VLMs (7B–34B), comparisons against five recent SOTA hallucination-mitigation methods, component ablations, agent-turn scaling analyses, and hyperparameter sensitivity — a broad and convincing experimental suite showing consistent (2.4–4.4%) improvements.

Practical attention to deployment: a Key-Norm alternative is provided for models with Flash-Attention where attention scores are inaccessible, and its performance gap is empirically quantified (Table 7).
The proposed HS metric attempts to quantify both severity and propagation of hallucinations, addressing a gap in MAS-level hallucination evaluation.
weaknesses: 'Plug-and-play' is somewhat overstated: the visual relay token contextualization requires training a transformer block with a two-stage pipeline (Table 8), so the method is not purely inference-time; the cost and data composition of this training are under-discussed.

The headline metric (HS score) is self-proposed and relies on a judge model; its validity, correlation with human judgment, and robustness to judge choice are not validated, and many conclusions (e.g., '30–40% HS reduction') rest on it.

Hyperparameters (ω, τ, α1, α2) appear to be selected by directly optimizing performance on the evaluation benchmarks (Tables 9–11), raising concerns about test-set tuning and generalization of the reported gains; no separate validation split is described.

The causal link between attention allocation to vision tokens and hallucination snowballing is argued mainly through correlation (Figures 1b–1c); the analysis supports plausibility but does not definitively establish causation, and the attention-based narrative inherits the known limits of attention-as-explanation.

Gains on comprehensive benchmarks (MME, MMBench, MM-Vet) are modest (~2–3%), so the contribution is mostly concentrated on hallucination benchmarks; statistical significance/variance over runs is not reported.

Method details (e.g., exact reallocation mask construction across layers, interaction of relay tokens with original vision tokens in the context) could be described more precisely, affecting reproducibility despite the promised code release.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a genuinely interesting and novel failure mode — multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing — that is distinct from well-studied single-agent hallucination, and grounds it in a mechanistic analysis (turn-, layer-, and token-wise attention dynamics).

The diagnostic analyses are thorough and convincing: layer-wise attention trends across agent turns (Fig. 2), controlled vision-token ablations across shallow/middle/deep layers (Tables 1, 16), and visualization of unimodal tokens (Fig. 4) provide solid evidence for why middle-layer unimodal vision tokens matter.

ViF is a principled, insight-driven solution: relaying visual evidence via selected unimodal tokens rather than lossy text, plus attention reallocation, with a practical Key-Norm alternative for Flash-Attention models where attention scores are unavailable.

Very broad evaluation: 8-12 benchmarks spanning images, multi-image, and video; 10 base VLMs (7B-34B); 4 MAS structures; comparisons against five strong training-free hallucination-mitigation baselines; ablations, hyper-parameter sensitivity, adversarial-input tests, combination with other methods, and efficiency measurements.
Honest limitations section acknowledging missing model families (InternVL, Llama 3, Ovis) and sizes, and source code is stated to be publicly available.
weaknesses: The headline snowballing reduction (30-40% HS score) is measured with the authors' own newly proposed HS metric, scored by an LLM judge (GPT-5). This introduces circularity: the primary quantitative claim of the paper rests on a self-defined, judge-dependent metric rather than established benchmarks, and statistical variance/significance of judge scores is only partially validated (94% discrepancies below 10% on one benchmark).

Gains on the original, established metrics are modest (avg ~2.4-3.8%), and on some benchmarks (CHAIR) performance actually slightly degrades; given the added component, training overhead, and per-turn complexity, the practical benefit is not uniformly strong.

The causal link between attention allocation reduction and hallucination snowballing is correlational; the paper shows co-occurrence (Fig. 1c) but does not establish that attention degradation causes snowballing, and alternative explanations (e.g., context length effects, instruction-token dilution) are not fully ruled out.

The MAS setting is somewhat artificial: the same image plus progressively harder questions across turns on single-image QA/captioning benchmarks. Whether the phenomenon and the fix transfer to more realistic agent workflows (tool use, heterogeneous agents, task decomposition) remains untested.

Consistency issues in methodology: some models use attention scores while others (Flash-Attention models) use the Key-Norm surrogate with heuristic buffer tokens, so results across models are not produced under a single uniform mechanism; the transformer-based relay token contextualizer requires training, which slightly weakens the 'training-free / lightweight' framing.

Writing and presentation have minor issues (e.g., typos such as 'Eixsting', 'visual hallucanation', 'V = V − V⊘' notation inconsistencies), and Table 2's dense presentation is hard to parse; per-agent-turn decomposition of scores is relegated to figures.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and potentially important failure mode (visual hallucination propagation/snowballing in VLM-based multi-agent systems) that is distinct from single-agent hallucination work.

The attention-based diagnostic analyses (turn-, layer-, and token-wise) are reasonably thorough, and the token-dropping ablations across shallow/middle/deep layers across six VLMs provide supporting evidence for the claimed mechanism.

Empirical coverage is broad: ten base VLMs (7B-34B), four MAS topologies, and twelve benchmarks, with ablations, hyper-parameter sensitivity, efficiency measurements, and an adversarial-input analysis in the appendix.
The proposed method is lightweight and the Key-Norm alternative for Flash-Attention models where attention scores are inaccessible is a practical consideration.
weaknesses: The multi-agent experimental setting appears artificial and its ecological validity is questionable. Benchmarks such as POPE, CHAIR, and MMHal-Bench are fundamentally single-image, single-question tasks; simulating 20 'agent turns' over the same image/question manufactures the snowballing phenomenon rather than observing it in realistic MAS workloads (collaborative reasoning, tool use, etc.). The paper never demonstrates that this failure mode arises in a genuinely multi-task, multi-agent pipeline.

The claimed causal link between visual attention degradation and hallucination snowballing is not established; the analyses are correlational. Attention reduction and error growth co-occur, but the paper provides no intervention (beyond its own fix) that directly manipulates attention and shows hallucination changes accordingly.

The headline 'Hallucination Snowballing (HS)' metric is proposed by the authors, evaluated by GPT-5 as judge, and is precisely the metric on which the method shows its most dramatic gains (~35-40% reduction), while gains on standard metrics are modest (~2-3% average, with MME/CHAIR changes often smaller than typical run-to-run variance). There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere, making the small improvements on original metrics difficult to trust.

Missing the most informative baselines. There is no comparison against simply re-sending the full image (or a re-encoded version) to downstream agents, random visual-token relay without the unimodal selection, or established multi-agent communication/re-anchoring strategies. All compared methods (MemVR, VISTA, FarSight, DeCo, TAME) are single-agent hallucination methods retrofitted to MAS, which makes the comparison somewhat strawman-like; the claim that they 'even underperform the baseline' is surprising and under-explained.

The method's key component requires access to attention scores, which is incompatible with Flash-Attention 2/3 used by most modern models; the Key-Norm fallback loses tokens and requires heuristic buffer patches, and Figure 13 shows the core attention-peak analysis for Qwen2/2.5-VL relies on this proxy, weakening the universality of the mechanistic claims.

Training details for the lightweight transformer block (Eq. 1) are thin: the training data, its relationship to the evaluation benchmarks, and the risk of data contamination/benchmark-specific tuning are not discussed, despite this module being trainable (Table 10).

Presentation issues undermine confidence: typos ('Eixsting', 'hallucanation', 'evdences'), a missing URL after 'publicly available at:', inconsistent figure numbering, and dense tables (e.g., Table 2) that are hard to parse. The abstract/introduction overstate the contributions relative to what is a well-engineered but incremental attention-reallocation technique.

The absolute magnitude of the 'unimodal token' population is tiny (1.22% of tokens, dropping to 0.10%), and the improvements from the full method vs. simple compression variants (Table 11) are within ~1 point on several benchmarks, raising questions about how much of the benefit actually stems from the proposed mechanism versus simply injecting additional visual context.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a genuinely interesting and under-explored failure mode: visual hallucination snowballing in VLM-based multi-agent systems, and clearly distinguishes it from single-agent hallucination and prior text-only snowballing work (Zhang et al., 2024b; Zhong et al., 2024).

The diagnostic analyses (layer-wise, turn-wise, token-wise attention; token-dropping ablations across shallow/middle/deep layers in Table 1/16; proportion tracking in Figure 5/14) are systematic and directly motivate the method, and are replicated across six VLMs to avoid model-specific conclusions.

The proposed ViF is well-motivated and model-agnostic: selecting unimodal-attention vision tokens as visual relay tokens plus attention reallocation is a coherent mechanism that follows from the insights, with a practical Key-Norm alternative for Flash-Attention models.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive: 10 base models (7B-34B), 4 MAS structures, 12 benchmarks spanning image/multi-image/video, comparison against five SOTA hallucination mitigation baselines under the same MAS setting, ablations, hyper-parameter sensitivity, efficiency (latency/FLOPs) analysis, adversarial input robustness, and combination with other mitigation methods.
Efficiency overhead is honestly quantified (8-13% latency, 4-12% FLOPs) and shown to shrink for larger models, and the source code is stated to be publicly available.

The 'counterintuitive' observation that single-model hallucination mitigation methods can even hurt performance in MAS (Table 6) is an interesting finding that strengthens the case for a propagation-aware solution.
weaknesses: The MAS setup is somewhat artificial: all agents are the same base VLM collaborating over standard single-image benchmarks (POPE, CHAIR, etc.) that do not intrinsically require multi-agent collaboration, and the turn-based construction (up to 20 turns on binary questions) is far from realistic MAS deployments (tool use, heterogeneous roles, complex tasks). Generalization of the snowballing phenomenon and ViF to real agentic workloads is not demonstrated.

The causal link between attention-to-vision reduction and hallucination snowballing is correlational; the paper presents evidence of co-occurrence (Figure 1c) but no intervention that establishes attention reduction as the cause rather than a symptom of degradation.

The proposed HS metric relies on a proprietary LLM judge (GPT-5) with a hand-crafted prompt, and its main headline gains (30-40% HS reduction) are measured largely with this author-defined metric; judge circularity and sensitivity are only partially addressed with a single secondary judge experiment (Gemini 2.5 Pro on POPE only).

Absolute improvements on standard metrics are modest (roughly 1-3 points per benchmark, ~2.4-3.8% average), and the direction of some CHAIR changes is inconsistent across structures, so the practical significance relative to the added complexity and retraining (a trainable transformer block plus two-stage tuning) is debatable.

Components of the method are close to existing techniques (visual token selection/attention reallocation is well-trodden in single-VLM hallucination work, e.g., Liu et al. 2024c, Wen et al. 2025); the novelty lies mainly in transferring them to inter-agent message passing, which reduces the technical depth of the contribution.

Missing baselines/models acknowledged in Limitations (InternVL, Llama 3, Ovis, 3B and 72B models) leave the generality claims partially unverified, and no results on genuinely multi-agent collaboration benchmarks are provided.

Writing has noticeable typos and polish issues (e.g., 'hallucanation', 'Eixsting', 'hallucanation benchmarks'), and several design choices (omega, tau, alpha values) appear tuned on the evaluation benchmarks without a separate validation split, raising mild overfitting concerns.
